title: Start here: NOAI, IOAI and how to prepare
tagline: Your map from zero to finalist
summary: What the National Olympiad in AI is, who can enter and how, how the Prelim and Final work and are scored, where it leads (NTU selection and IOAI 2027 in Singapore), and how to study this course efficiently.
syllabus: NOAI 2027 Preliminary Round: Fri 19 Feb 2027, 150 MCQs in 90 min, five domains, no calculator, no penalty
NOAI 2027 Final: Fri 5 Mar 2027, 20 MCQs + 3 Python programming tasks (Theoretical Concept + Practical Implementation)
Eligibility and school-based registration; direct-entry route for non-MOE students
NTU IOAI selection and training; IOAI syllabus overview (Theory / Practice / Both)

lessons.title: What NOAI is and where it leads
lessons.summary: The four stages from your school's computer lab to IOAI 2027 in Singapore, who can enter, and how to register.
objectives: You can describe the four stages from Prelim to IOAI
You can state the key 2027 dates
You know how you register (through your school, or by emailing AISG if you are not in an MOE school)

concepts.name: The selection funnel
concepts.explain: NOAI is a series of filters. Anyone eligible can sit the Preliminary Round; the top 150 sit the Final; about the top 60 are invited to NTU's selection test and training; a small team represents Singapore at IOAI. Each stage tests something different, so preparation changes as you go.
concepts.analogy: Like the NDP fun pack queue becoming a stadium seat: lots of people at the gate, fewer at each checkpoint, and each checkpoint checks something different.

visual.shows: A vertical funnel with four bands (Prelim, Final, NTU selection and camp, IOAI team), each labelled with date, format and the number who pass through; small dots stream down and stop at each band.
visual.interaction: Play/pause the stream; click a band to expand a card with its format (e.g. 150 MCQs, 90 min) and what it rewards (speed recall vs implementation vs open-ended modelling).
visual.aha: Each stage rewards a different skill, so you train breadth and speed first, then from-scratch coding, then real-model building.

concepts.name: The countdown timeline
concepts.explain: The dates are fixed: Prelim Friday 19 Feb 2027, Final Friday 5 Mar 2027, NTU selection test 8 May 2027, IOAI 4 to 10 July 2027 in Singapore. Working backwards from those dates tells you how many weeks you have for each part of this course.
concepts.analogy: Like planning revision backwards from the O-level timetable rather than forwards from today.

visual.shows: A horizontal timeline from Oct 2026 to Jul 2027 with milestone pins and a draggable 'today' marker; weeks remaining to each milestone are shown as labelled spans.
visual.interaction: Drag the 'today' marker; the weeks-left readouts and a suggested 'what to be studying now' label update.
visual.aha: The Prelim is only about 18 weeks away from mid-October, and the Final is just two weeks after it, so Final coding practice must start before the Prelim.

concepts.name: Who can enter and how to register
concepts.explain: Registration goes through your school, not through you. Full-time MOE students under 20 sign up via their school's NOAI teacher representative. Home-schooled, in-between-schools and private-school students can email AISG directly before the deadline. Only Singapore Citizens and PRs can be picked for the IOAI team.
concepts.analogy: Like joining an inter-school competition: your CCA teacher submits the team list, and you cannot walk in on the day.

visual.shows: A short form with toggles for school type, age and citizenship. The result card gives your registration route, deadline and whether you can reach the IOAI team.
visual.interaction: Flip the toggles, for example 'international school' or 'PR', and watch the route and deadline change.
visual.aha: Anyone eligible can compete in NOAI. Citizenship only matters for the final national team.

checkpoint_focus: Selection funnel: Prelim → top 150 Final → about top 60 at NTU → IOAI team
Key dates: 19 Feb, 5 Mar, 8 May, 4 to 10 Jul 2027

lessons.title: The exam format and how it is scored
lessons.summary: Exactly what the Prelim and Final look like, and the scoring facts that should shape your strategy.
objectives: You can describe the Prelim (150 MCQs, 90 minutes, about 36 s each, no calculator, no penalty)
You can explain why you should answer every question
You can describe the two sections of the Final

concepts.name: The 36-second budget
concepts.explain: 90 minutes for 150 questions gives 5400 / 150 = 36 seconds per question. Some questions take 10 seconds, others 90, so the budget is an average you manage with checkpoints, not a rule for each question.
concepts.analogy: Like a 2.4 km run: you check your lap splits so you do not sprint the first lap and walk the last.

visual.shows: A progress bar of 150 question cells and a clock; a mixture of quick, medium and slow questions is simulated with your chosen pace and 'skip threshold'.
visual.interaction: Slide 'seconds before I skip and come back' and 'average seconds on easy questions'; see how many questions you reach and your projected score.
visual.aha: Capping time on hard questions reaches more questions and scores more than solving every question in order.

concepts.name: No negative marking means never leave a blank
concepts.explain: Each correct answer earns 1 mark and wrong answers lose nothing, so a blind guess on a four-option question is worth 1/4 of a mark on average. Eliminating one or two options raises that to 1/3 or 1/2.
concepts.analogy: Like a free lucky draw ticket: you would never throw it away unused.

visual.shows: Four option cards and a bar showing expected marks from guessing, plus a tally over 20 unanswered questions.
visual.interaction: Click options to eliminate them (0, 1 or 2) and change the number of blanks; expected marks update (e.g. 20 blanks guessed blind ≈ 5 marks).
visual.aha: Leaving blanks throws away free marks; eliminating even one option makes each guess 33% more valuable.

concepts.name: The Final: theory plus implementation
concepts.explain: The top 150 sit a Final with 20 harder MCQs (often reading code) and 3 programming tasks in Jupyter notebooks, where you implement algorithms from scratch with NumPy or PyTorch. Past tasks include gradient descent, k-means, RAG, gradient boosting, a U-Net fix with mean IoU, and attention.
concepts.analogy: Like a driving test: the theory test gets you in, but you pass by actually driving.

visual.shows: A two-column board for 2025 and 2026 Finals listing each task, its marks and the course module that teaches it, linked by lines.
visual.interaction: Hover or tap a task to highlight the modules it needs; click to jump to that module.
visual.aha: Every past Final task is a classic algorithm you can practise in advance, so the Final is very preparable.

checkpoint_focus: Expected value of guessing with no penalty

lessons.title: How to study so it sticks
lessons.summary: Retrieval practice, spacing and a personal plan to cover the course before 19 Feb 2027.
objectives: You can explain why testing yourself beats re-reading
You can build a weekly plan that finishes the course before the Prelim

concepts.name: The forgetting curve and spaced review
concepts.explain: Memory fades quickly after you learn something, but each well-timed review makes it fade more slowly. Testing yourself (retrieval) strengthens memory more than reading the same notes again.
concepts.analogy: Like topping up an EZ-Link card before it runs out: small, regular top-ups beat one big panic top-up at the gantry.

visual.shows: A retention-versus-days plot with an exponential decay curve; each review resets retention to near 100% and flattens the next decay.
visual.interaction: Click on the time axis to add review sessions; see retention on exam day (19 Feb) change.
visual.aha: Three spaced reviews keep retention high on exam day, while one late cram does not.

concepts.name: Your personal study plan
concepts.explain: The course has a fixed number of lessons and minutes. Dividing them by the weeks you have and the hours you can give each week tells you your pace, and where you need to start earlier or cut back. Because the Final is only two weeks after the Prelim, start the Final labs (from-scratch coding) well before 19 Feb instead of waiting for Prelim results.
concepts.analogy: Like planning a CCA season: training load is set by how many weeks remain before the competition.

visual.shows: A Gantt-style bar of all parts laid over the weeks until 19 Feb 2027, with the Final and NTU dates marked.
visual.interaction: Set start date and hours per week with sliders; the parts stretch or compress, and a warning appears if the plan finishes after the Prelim.
visual.aha: Even 5 hours a week covers the course if you start now; waiting a month means doubling the weekly load.

concepts.name: How a lesson on this site works
concepts.explain: Every lesson follows the same arc: analogy, an interactive visual, the formal idea, a worked example, code, common mistakes, exam tips and a checkpoint quiz. Knowing the arc helps you use each part on purpose.
concepts.analogy: Like a hawker stall's set meal: the same courses every time, so you know what is coming.

visual.shows: A miniature lesson page with labelled regions (analogy, visual, formal idea, steps, code, mistake, exam tip, checkpoint).
visual.interaction: Click a region to read how to use it (e.g. 'predict before you drag').
visual.aha: Predicting what the visual will do before you touch it is the fastest way to learn from it.
